title: Session 1 – Introduction to Data-Driven Decisions & Data Ethics

blocks.text: Good decisions combine data and intuition: data validates and informs assumptions, but it does not generate the ideas worth testing (Marc Randolph, Netflix). The goal is a culture of "The data shows…" instead of "I think…".
Data and marketing analytics can be structured along a framework (Wedel & Kannan, 2016):
children: Types of data: structured vs. unstructured, Big Data
Analytics and analytical methods
Implementing data and analytics in companies
Applications: personalisation, CRM, marketing mix, privacy and security

blocks.text: Big Data refers to the explosion in the quantity (and sometimes quality) of available data due to advances in data recording and storage. It is characterised by the 5 Vs: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity and Value.
Four types of analytics move from information over insights to decision/action:
children: Descriptive: What happened in the business?
Diagnostic: Why is something happening?
Predictive: What is likely to happen in the future?
Prescriptive: So what? Now what? What is required to do more?

blocks.text: Three research types lead from descriptive to diagnostic analytics:
children: Exploratory research: ambiguous problem ("Our sales are declining… why?"); flexible, versatile, front end of the research design; expert surveys, pilot surveys, qualitative research, qualitatively analysed secondary data
Descriptive research: aware of the problem ("Who buys our products?"); prior hypotheses, preplanned and structured; surveys, panels, observation, quantitatively analysed secondary data
Causal research: clearly defined problem ("Will customers buy more after a website change?"); manipulation of independent variables and control of others; experiments

blocks.text: Companies create value through data in three ways (Mazzei & Noble, 2017):
children: Data as a tool: active data collection and internal analytical capabilities to improve product development, marketing, sales, distribution, customer service
Data as an industry: providers of big-data products/services, technology and data-as-a-service
Data as a strategy: big data drives competitive strategy, new business models and ecosystems (e.g. Rolls-Royce)
Starbucks Deep Brew (reinforcement learning, next-best offer): from segment-based campaigns to an individual, real-time journey; from short-term response to long-term value maximisation
Sephora Virtual Artist + agentic AI Beauty Advisor: from reactive personalisation to an autonomous digital sales agent; from A/B testing to continuous real-time adaptation

blocks.text: Surveillance capitalism (Zuboff) claims human experience as free raw material for hidden practices of extraction, prediction and sales and aims at behavioural modification. Byung-Chul Han calls Big Data a psychopolitical instrument; Cathy O'Neil warns against blind faith in algorithms.

children: Physical privacy vs. information privacy
GDPR (May 2018): clear language, affirmative consent, transparency, stronger rights, stronger enforcement
Kollnig et al. (2021): limited change in third-party tracking after GDPR, further concentration (gatekeepers)
Digital Services Act: cookie banners, online advertising, illegal content, algorithmic transparency; strictest rules above 45 million monthly users

blocks.text: Susskind's Digital Republic proposes four principles: preservation, domination, democracy and parsimony.

Information, especially facts or numbers, collected to be examined and used to help decision-making; or information in electronic form that can be stored and used by a computer (Cambridge Dictionary).
The explosion in the quantity (and sometimes quality) of available and potentially relevant data, largely the result of recent advances in data recording and storage technology (Diebold, 2000).
The process of examining datasets in order to draw conclusions about the information they contain, increasingly with the aid of specialised systems and software.
A new economic order that claims human experience as free raw material for hidden commercial practices of extraction, prediction and sales (Zuboff, 2019).
The difference between what people think they should do to protect their privacy and what they actually do.

Note from the revision session: except for session 1, any in-class exercise can become an exam exercise – but session 1 concepts (analytics types, research types, data ethics) can still appear in the true/false part.
How have data strategies evolved since McKinsey's 2013 article? Think of AI agents, real-time personalisation and regulation (GDPR, DSA).
